newsitem.title: UK: BA resists slot demands for American deal.
newsitem.headline: BA resists slot demands for American deal.

text.p: British Airways Plc said on Tuesday it remained hopeful it would win regulatory approvals for its alliance with American Airlines.

But the world's biggest international airline made clear it was still opposing demands from regulators and rival airlines that it give up hundreds of runway slots at London Heathrow to make room for competition.

Chief executive Robert Ayling told the company's annual meeting he believed progress was at last being made in the protracted negotiations and a way could still be found to get round the vexed issue of making room for competition at Heathrow, Europe's top international hub.

But he dismissed speculation that BA was now willing to give up the 168 weekly slots at Heathrow, which were proposed last year by the British competition authorities and subsequently rejected as too few by European Union competition commissioner Karel Van Miert.
Ayling was asked by a shareholder at Tuesday's meeting to give assurances that BA would stop at 168 slots -- equivalent to 12 daily return flights -- in its negotiations with regulators.
"The 168 slots was not our idea it was an idea that came from the (British) Director General of Fair Trading and the British Government has never commented on it," he replied.
"I think 168 slots is already a very large number of slots which makes it very difficult to proceed," he added.
Recent newspaper reports have suggested that in order to satisfy opposition in Europe and the U.S. the BA and American alliance would have to give up at least twice that number of slots.

But Ayling and BA chairman Sir Colin Marshall told the annual meeting they were confident that concerns about competition at Heathrow could be overcome in time for the next summer season, starting in April.
"Approval for our alliance hangs on the problem of achieving greater access to a congested Heathrow for our transatlantic competitors," Marshall said.
"We are in continuing dialogue with the respective authorities and hopeful of a satisfactory outcome."
Later Ayling told shareholders: "We are making headway. We are not absolutely certain we will get approval but I remain hopeful."
